Handful
HAND-ful
n.
From hand and full: as much as the hand will grasp. Webster 1828: as much as the hand will grasp or contain; a small quantity or number. In Scripture the handful is the unit of the memorial offering and the standing measure of God’s sufficiency in famine.

Biblical Definition

A handful is what is left when everything else is gone, and Scripture keeps putting it at the hinge of the story. The widow of Zarephath states her situation as a death sentence: I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die (1 Kings 17:12). She is asked to give that handful away first, and the barrel does not fail through the famine. The same measure is the appointed portion in the meat offering: he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar (Leviticus 2:2). God takes a handful and calls it the memorial; the rest feeds the priests. The Preacher weighs the handful against the full grasp and prefers it: Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:6). Against all three stands the boast of Benhadad, who reckoned Samaria itself would not yield handfuls for all the people that follow me (1 Kings 20:10) — and who lost.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HANDFUL as as much as the hand will grasp or contain; a small quantity or number; a palmful.

expand to see more

HANDFUL, n. — As much as the hand will grasp or contain.

A small quantity or number; as, a handful of men.

A palm; a hand’s breadth; four inches.

As much as the arms can embrace or hold.

From hand and full; compare the Hebrew qomets, the closed hand, the priest’s portion.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 17:12 — "And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die."

Leviticus 2:2 — "And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar, to be an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD:"

Ecclesiastes 4:6 — "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit."

1 Kings 20:10 — "And Benhadad sent unto him, and said, The gods do so unto me, and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people that follow me."

Modern Corruption

The Zarephath narrative is a favourite text of the prosperity teachers, who read the widow’s handful as seed sown for a return; the passage is about the sufficiency of God in famine, not a technique for obtaining abundance.

expand to see more

1 Kings 17 is regularly preached as a transaction: give your last handful to the man of God and God will multiply it back to you. That reading has the direction of the covenant reversed. The widow is not investing; she is obeying a prophetic word in a famine that God Himself had declared, and what she receives is not wealth but daily sustenance — a barrel that does not waste and a cruse that does not fail, exactly enough, for as long as the drought lasts. Prosperity teaching (Hagin, Copeland, and the modern seed-faith industry) turns this into a law of return, and in doing so makes God a mechanism and the giver the real agent. The Reformed doctrine of providence says the opposite: God gives daily bread as He sees fit, and the widow’s security lay in His word, not in the size of her gift. Our Lord Himself cites this very widow in Luke 4:26 — and He cites her as an instance of sovereign election, not of successful giving.

Leviticus 2:2 guards a second point. God requires a handful, not the whole; the memorial portion is burnt and the remainder feeds Aaron’s sons. The token is not a discount on obedience but the appointed form of it, and offering more than commanded is no more acceptable than offering less — Nadab and Abihu are two chapters away. This is the regulative principle in its Levitical form: what God commands is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted, in the offering as in the worship. Ecclesiastes 4:6 then applies the same measure to ordinary life, and the verdict is against the full grasp: a handful with quietness beats two hands full with vexation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qomets (H7062), the closed hand, a handful; kaph (H3709), the hollow of the hand; shoal (H8168), a handful as a measure; malo kaph, the fulness of the palm.

expand to see more

Hebrew qomets (H7062) — the closed hand and so a handful; the priest’s memorial portion of the meat offering (Leviticus 2:2).

Hebrew kaph (H3709) — the hollow or palm of the hand; an handful of meal in a barrel (1 Kings 17:12).

Hebrew shoal (H8168) — a handful as a formal measure, the same word as the hollow of God’s hand in Isaiah 40:12.

Hebrew azkarah (H234) — the memorial, the name given to the handful burnt on the altar (Leviticus 2:2).

Hebrew nachath (H5183) — quietness, rest; the thing that makes the single handful better (Ecclesiastes 4:6).

Usage

"An handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse (1 Kings 17:12) — the widow is asked to give the last of it away first."

"He shall take thereout his handful... and burn the memorial of it (Leviticus 2:2) — God takes a handful and calls it the memorial."

"Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail (Ecclesiastes 4:6) — the verdict is against the full grasp."
